title: 22. Interview: HAProxy
summary: Interview Q&A for HAProxy — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 HAProxy interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why is HAProxy often chosen over NGINX for high-throughput Layer 4 load balancing?
**Answer:** HAProxy was designed from the start as a pure load balancer (no web serving, no static files), so its internals are optimized for one thing: moving bytes between frontends and backends at maximum speed and reliability. Several specific advantages. (1) **Lower per-connection overhead** — HAProxy's event loop is highly tuned for connection handling, with very low per-connection memory (a few KB) and minimal syscall overhead; benchmarks consistently show HAProxy sustaining higher req/s than NGINX for pure L4 proxying. (2) **Better load-balancing algorithms** — HAProxy offers `leastconn` with proper tracking, dynamic weight changes at runtime, slow-start for freshly-recovered backends, and `random` with power-of-two-choices; NGINX's open-source algorithms are simpler (RR, LC, ip_hash). (3) **Best-in-class stats page** — HAProxy's stats UI shows per-frontend/backend/server request rates, connection counts, error counts, latency percentiles, and server health in real-time, with interactive controls (drain a server, change weight); NGINX open-source has minimal stats (needs Plus or third-party modules). (4) **Runtime API** — HAProxy's Unix socket admin API allows live backend changes without reload; NGINX open-source requires reload or third-party modules. (5) **Reputation for reliability** — HAProxy's bug rate is famously low; sites like Stack Overflow and Reddit trust it for their critical path. NGINX is better when you need its broader feature set (web serving, HTTP/2, caching, Lua); HAProxy is better when you need pure LB performance and observability.
**Visual:**
```
NGINX strengths: web server + proxy + LB + HTTP/2 + Lua + caching
HAProxy strengths: pure LB perf, best stats, runtime API, dynamic weights,
                   leastconn with slow-start, ACL-based routing
pattern: NGINX edge -> HAProxy backend L4 (Reddit, StackOverflow)
```

### Q2. What is an ACL in HAProxy, and how does it differ from NGINX's `location` blocks?
**Answer:** An HAProxy ACL is a named condition that matches some aspect of the request: `path_beg /api/` (URL prefix), `hdr(host) -i admin.example.com` (Host header, case-insensitive), `src 192.168.0.0/16` (source IP CIDR), `ssl_fc` (request came in over SSL), `req.fhdr(user-agent) -m sub mobile` (header substring match), and many more. ACLs are combined with `if`/`unless` clauses on `use_backend`, `http-request`, `redirect`, etc., allowing fine-grained routing. For example: `use_backend api_v2 if { path_beg /api/v2/ }` or `use_backend mobile if { req.hdr(User-Agent) -m sub mobile } { src -f mobile_ips.txt }`. The key difference from NGINX's `location` blocks is composability: HAProxy ACLs are first-class named values that you can combine with `||` (or), `&&` (and), `!` (not), and reference across multiple directives; NGINX `location` blocks are nested patterns, and combining conditions requires `if` directives (which NGINX's docs famously call "if is evil" due to unpredictable behavior). ACLs let you express arbitrarily complex routing rules declaratively without Lua code. The trade-off: HAProxy's ACL syntax is its own DSL with a learning curve, while NGINX's `location` is more familiar to most ops engineers.
**Visual:**
```
HAProxy ACL:
  acl is_admin    hdr(host) -i admin.example.com
  acl is_internal src 10.0.0.0/8
  use_backend admin if is_admin is_internal    # AND
  use_backend admin if { is_admin || is_internal }  # OR (alt syntax)

NGINX location (no easy composition):
  server { server_name admin.example.com; location / { proxy_pass admin; } }
  (combining Host + src requires 'if' - "if is evil")
```

### Q3. How does HAProxy's hot reload work, and why is it considered superior to NGINX's?
**Answer:** Both HAProxy and NGINX do zero-downtime reloads, but HAProxy's mechanism is more transparent. `systemctl reload haproxy` causes the master process to re-exec with the new config. The new process inherits the listening sockets from the old process (via `SO_REUSEPORT` or the `fd@` inherit-fd mechanism), so the new process is immediately ready to accept connections on the same port. The old process stops accepting new connections and drains in-flight requests; once all in-flight requests complete, it exits. The handoff is atomic at the kernel level — even mid-handshake TCP connections are preserved. The reason HAProxy's reload is considered superior: (1) it's faster — the socket transfer is a single syscall, not a process fork-then-rebind dance; (2) it's more reliable — there's no window where the listening socket might be closed (NGINX's reload briefly forks new workers and the old workers can take up to 60s to drain); (3) it integrates with the runtime API — if you only need to change a server's weight or add/remove a backend, you can do it via the Unix socket without a reload at all. NGINX open-source requires a reload for any upstream change; HAProxy's runtime API handles most operational changes live.
**Visual:**
```
HAProxy reload:
  master re-exec with new config
  new process inherits listening sockets (SO_REUSEPORT) -> instant ready
  old process drains in-flight, exits
  no client-visible downtime, atomic at kernel level

NGINX reload:
  master re-reads config, forks NEW workers
  master SIGTERMs OLD workers
  OLD: stop accept, drain (up to 60s), exit
  NEW: accept new conns
  (long-lived conns on OLD workers linger)
```

### Q4. What is HAProxy's runtime API and what can you do with it?
**Answer:** HAProxy's runtime API is a Unix socket (configured with `stats socket /run/haproxy/admin.sock mode 660 level admin`) that accepts plain-text commands for live operational changes without a config reload. You interact via `socat` or `nc`: `echo "show servers state api_v1" | socat /run/haproxy/admin.sock -`. Common commands: `set server <backend>/<server> state drain|maint|ready` (drain a server for maintenance), `set server <backend>/<server> weight 50` (change weight live), `add server` / `del server` (some versions), `show servers state` (list all backends and their states), `show stat` (CSV stats dump), `clear counters` (reset stats), `show sess` (list active sessions), `shutdown session <id>` (kill a stuck session). This is the operational gold for production incidents — you can drain a misbehaving backend in one command without a reload, then bring it back when fixed. It's also how dynamic environments integrate with HAProxy: Kubernetes ingress controllers, Consul-template, and HashiCorp's tools all use the runtime API to keep HAProxy's backend pool in sync with service discovery, avoiding reloads entirely. HAProxy 2.0+ also added a REST "data plane API" that wraps the runtime socket in HTTP, making it easier to call from cloud-native tools.
**Visual:**
```
$ echo "set server api_v1/s3 state drain" | socat /run/haproxy/admin.sock -
$ echo "set server api_v1/s3 weight 0"    | socat /run/haproxy/admin.sock -
$ echo "show servers state api_v1"        | socat /run/haproxy/admin.sock -
be_id  be_name  srv_id  srv_name  srv_addr   srv_status  srv_weight
1      api_v1   1       s1        10.0.0.1   UP          1
1      api_v1   2       s2        10.0.0.2   UP          1
1      api_v1   3       s3        10.0.0.3   DRAIN       0
```

### Q5. How do active and passive health checks work in HAProxy, and how do they differ?
**Answer:** **Active health checks** are configured with `option httpchk GET /healthz` and `server s1 10.0.0.1:8080 check inter 2s rise 2 fall 3`. HAProxy periodically (every `inter` seconds, default 2s) sends an HTTP request to the configured path on the server; if it gets a 2xx/3xx response within the timeout, the check passes. A server needs `rise` (default 2) consecutive successes to transition from DOWN to UP, and `fall` (default 3) consecutive failures to transition from UP to DOWN. This catches total failures (server dead, port closed) within `fall * inter` seconds (6 seconds by default). **Passive health checks** are configured with `observe layer7` (HTTP-level) or `observe layer4` (TCP-level) on the server line. HAProxy observes real traffic outcomes — if a server returns consecutive 5xx errors or connection failures to real client requests, HAProxy marks it down immediately, without waiting for the next active probe. This catches transient failures (a server that's slow but still responds to /healthz with 200) within 1-2 seconds. The production pattern is both: active for steady-state verification, passive for fast failure detection. HAProxy also supports **agent checks** (`agent-check` + `agent-port`) where the backend runs a separate TCP agent (port 12345) that returns its app-level health ("up", "down", "drain", or a numeric weight) — useful for "the server is up but my database connection is broken, mark me down" scenarios.
**Visual:**
```
active:    HAProxy --GET /healthz--> server (every 2s)
           3 failures -> DOWN (6s detection)
           catches: server dead, port closed

passive:   client req -> server -> 500, 500, 500 -> DOWN (immediate)
           catches: server alive but returning errors

agent:     HAProxy --TCP--> server:12345 -> "drain" or "50%"
           catches: app-level health (e.g., DB unreachable)
```

### Q6. How does HAProxy do SSL termination with SNI, and what's the difference between termination and passthrough?
**Answer:** **SSL termination** means HAProxy decrypts the TLS connection and proxies plain HTTP to the backend. Configured with `bind *:443 ssl crt /etc/haproxy/certs/api.pem crt /etc/haproxy/certs/admin.pem` — HAProxy presents the matching certificate based on the SNI (Server Name Indication) field in the ClientHello, allowing multiple hostnames on one IP/port. Once decrypted, HAProxy can do HTTP-level features: ACL-based routing, header manipulation, sticky cookies, stats. **TLS passthrough** means HAProxy doesn't decrypt; it reads just enough of the ClientHello to extract the SNI, then forwards the encrypted bytes to the backend, which terminates TLS itself. Configured with `mode tcp` + `tcp-request inspect-delay 5s` + `use_backend api if { req.ssl_sni -i api.example.com }`. Passthrough is used when backends must terminate their own TLS — for end-to-end encryption (zero trust), for client-certificate authentication that the backend verifies, or when certs can't be shared with the LB. The trade-off: termination enables HTTP-level features (richer routing, header manipulation, stats) but means the LB sees decrypted traffic (a security/ compliance concern); passthrough preserves end-to-end encryption but loses HTTP-level features and is limited to SNI-based routing. HAProxy is unusually good at mixing both in the same config — a single HAProxy instance can terminate for some hostnames and passthrough for others, while NGINX requires separate `server` blocks.
**Visual:**
```
termination:  client ==TLS==> HAProxy (decrypt) ==HTTP==> backend
              + ACL routing, header manipulation, stats
              - LB sees decrypted traffic

passthrough:  client ==TLS==> HAProxy (read SNI) ==TLS==> backend (decrypt)
              + end-to-end encryption
              - only SNI-based routing, no HTTP inspection

HAProxy can mix both in one config (NGINX needs separate servers).
```

### Q7. What is HAProxy's slow-start feature and why does it matter?
**Answer:** When a backend server comes back online (after a restart, deploy, or recovery from a failure), HAProxy's default behavior is to immediately route its full share of traffic to it. This causes a thundering-herd problem: the freshly-recovered server is hit with its full traffic quota while its caches are cold, JIT is uncompiled, connection pools are empty, and DB prepared statements are gone — the server gets overloaded, response times spike, and it may fail its health check and go down again (flapping). **Slow-start** (`slowstart 30s` on the server line) fixes this: when a server transitions from DOWN to UP, its effective weight ramps up gradually over the configured duration (e.g., 30 seconds). At t=0 it gets a tiny fraction of its normal traffic; at t=15s it gets half; at t=30s it gets full traffic. This gives the server time to warm up its caches, JIT-compile, and establish connection pools under gradually-increasing load. Slow-start is critical for: (1) post-deploy restarts where the new code is the same but caches are cold; (2) post-failure recovery where the server is alive but still catching up on state; (3) databases where the query plan cache and buffer pool need warming. NGINX open-source lacks slow-start (it's an NGINX Plus feature); HAProxy has had it for years. The trade-off: during slow-start, the other servers in the pool carry more traffic, so you need enough headroom to absorb the temporary imbalance.
**Visual:**
```
without slow-start:
  srv3 comes back UP at t=0 -> full traffic immediately
  -> cache cold, JIT uncompiled, DB pools empty
  -> 5xx spike, health check fails -> srv3 DOWN again (flap)

with slowstart 30s:
  srv3 comes back UP at t=0 -> 5% traffic
                          t=10s -> 33%
                          t=20s -> 66%
                          t=30s -> 100% (warm now, stable)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your HAProxy shows a backend server as DOWN in the stats page, but the server is reachable via `curl` from the HAProxy host. What's going on?
**Answer:** Several possibilities. (1) **Health check path is wrong** — HAProxy is configured to GET `/healthz` but the server only responds on `/health`; the server returns 404 to HAProxy's probe (treated as failure), but `curl http://server/` returns 200. Fix: align the `option httpchk` path. (2) **Health check expects 2xx/3xx but server returns 401** — if your `/healthz` requires authentication, HAProxy's probe gets 401, treated as failure. Fix: configure `http-check expect status 200` or use a different unauthenticated path. (3) **Health check timeout too short** — `inter 2s` with a server that takes 3s to respond to /healthz (cold cache, GC pause); the probe times out. Fix: increase `timeout check` or `inter`. (4) **Passive health check marked it down** — `observe layer7` saw consecutive 5xx from real traffic and marked the server down, even though active probes pass. The stats page shows the reason code (e.g., "L7STS" for layer 7 status). (5) **Server was manually drained** — someone ran `set server api/s1 state drain` via the runtime API; it shows as DRAIN or MAINT, not UP. (6) **Slow-start still ramping** — server is technically UP but in slow-start; check the stats for the "throttle" indicator. (7) **Stick-table or session limits** — `maxconn` on the server is reached, so new connections are queued. Look at the stats page's "Status" column and the "Last" column (last check result) to diagnose. The fix is almost always in the stats page's per-server details.
**Visual:**
```
stats page:
  srv1  10.0.0.1:8080  UP    check: 200 OK  18ms
  srv2  10.0.0.2:8080  DOWN  check: 404     <- wrong path!
  srv3  10.0.0.3:8080  DOWN  reason: L7STS  <- passive (5xx storm)
  srv4  10.0.0.4:8080  MAINT                <- manually drained

curl from HAProxy host:
  curl http://10.0.0.2:8080/      -> 200 OK  (root path works)
  curl http://10.0.0.2:8080/healthz -> 404   (this is what HAProxy checks!)
fix: option httpchk GET /     (or whatever path returns 200)
```

### Q2. You need to deploy a new version of your API with zero downtime. How do you use HAProxy to do a canary deployment?
**Answer:** Use HAProxy's weighted round-robin to gradually shift traffic to the new backend pool. Setup: configure two backends — `api_v1` (current, 3 servers) and `api_v2` (new, 3 servers). Add a frontend ACL that routes a small fraction of traffic to `api_v2` based on something — `path_beg /api/v2/` for path-based canary, or a header-based ACL for opt-in canary (`hdr(x-canary) -i true`), or weighted routing across both pools. The cleanest approach for percentage-based canary: use two `use_backend` rules with weights, or put both pools in one backend with different weights (api_v1 servers at weight 10, api_v2 servers at weight 1 = ~9% canary). Steps: (1) Deploy api_v2 to a new pool, initially at weight 0 (no traffic). (2) Via the runtime API, `set server api_v2/v2_1 weight 1` — now ~9% of traffic goes to v2. (3) Monitor error rates, latency, business metrics for 30-60 minutes. (4) If healthy, gradually increase: `weight 2` (~17%), `weight 5` (~33%), `weight 10` (~50%). (5) If everything's good, ramp v2 to 100% and v1 to 0; once v1 has zero traffic, decommission it. (6) If at any point v2 shows problems, `set server api_v2/* weight 0` instantly rolls back. This is much faster than a deploy-then-rollback cycle and is what Netflix, Reddit, and others use for progressive delivery. HAProxy 2.0+ also supports traffic-splitting via `balance random` with `random_draws 2` for more sophisticated canary.
**Visual:**
```
Step 1: deploy v2, weight 0 (no traffic)
  api_v1: s1 w=10, s2 w=10, s3 w=10   (100% traffic)
  api_v2: v1 w=0,  v2 w=0,  v3 w=0    (0%)

Step 2: set v2 weight 1 (~9% canary)
  api_v2: v1 w=1   -> monitor 30 min

Step 3: ramp up
  v2 w=2 (~17%), w=5 (~33%), w=10 (~50%), w=30 (~75%), w=100 (100%)

Rollback (instant):
  set server api_v2/* weight 0   -> all traffic back to v1
```

### Q3. HAProxy is showing high latency on the stats page (p99 = 800ms) but the backend servers' own metrics show 50ms. What's happening?
**Answer:** The discrepancy means HAProxy is adding latency somewhere between receiving the request and getting the response — the backend serves in 50ms but HAProxy reports 800ms to the client. Common causes. (1) **Connection queue buildup** — if the backend's `maxconn` is reached, HAProxy queues requests in its own internal queue (`timeout queue` default 5s); the queued request waits 700ms for a slot, then takes 50ms on the backend = 750ms total. Check the stats page's "Queued" column. (2) **Connection reuse not enabled** — without `http-reuse safe` (or `always`), HAProxy opens a new TCP connection to the backend for each request, paying TCP handshake + TLS handshake (if backend is HTTPS) per request. Enable `http-reuse safe` and `option http-keep-alive`. (3) **DNS resolution delay** — if the backend is specified by hostname (`server s1 api.example.com:8080`) and `resolvers` aren't configured, HAProxy may re-resolve DNS per connection, adding 50-200ms. Use `resolvers` with a local DNS cache. (4) **Buffer size limits** — `tune.bufsize` default 16KB; if responses are larger, HAProxy buffers to disk, adding latency. Increase `tune.bufsize`. (5) **Health check storm** — too-frequent health checks on a busy backend can interfere with request handling; increase `inter` from 2s to 5s. (6) **CPU saturation on HAProxy host** — check `top` and `iostat`; if HAProxy itself is CPU-bound, scale out (add more HAProxy instances) or pin to more cores (`nbthread`).
**Visual:**
```
stats:           p99 = 800ms
backend logs:    p99 = 50ms
                 ^
                 +- 700ms added by HAProxy

cause #1: queue (maxconn reached)
  req -> HAProxy queue (700ms) -> backend (50ms) -> resp (total 750ms)
  fix: increase backend maxconn, scale backends

cause #2: no keep-alive (new TCP per req)
  req -> TCP handshake (50ms) -> backend (50ms) -> resp (100ms)
  fix: http-reuse safe, option http-keep-alive
```

### Q4. You're running HAProxy in front of a PostgreSQL cluster with one primary and three read replicas. How do you configure it?
**Answer:** Use two `backend` blocks in `mode tcp` — one for the primary (writes) and one for the replicas (reads), with separate frontends or ACLs to route. The application connects to a virtual IP that HAProxy load-balances. Sample config:

```haproxy
frontend pg_write
    bind *:5432
    mode tcp
    default_backend pg_primary

frontend pg_read
    bind *:5433
    mode tcp
    default_backend pg_replicas

backend pg_primary
    mode tcp
    option tcp-check
    tcp-check expect string r/w     # primary responds to "SHOW transaction_read_only" with "off"
    server pg1 10.0.0.1:5432 check

backend pg_replicas
    mode tcp
    balance roundrobin
    option tcp-check
    tcp-check expect string r/o     # replicas respond with "on"
    server pg2 10.0.0.2:5432 check
    server pg3 10.0.0.3:5432 check
    server pg4 10.0.0.4:5432 check
```

Key points: (1) `mode tcp` — PostgreSQL's binary protocol can't be parsed as HTTP, so HAProxy proxies raw bytes. (2) **Health check** uses `tcp-check` with a string expectation — a custom check that runs `SHOW transaction_read_only` and expects "off" for primary, "on" for replicas. If a replica is promoted to primary (failover), HAProxy's check fails for it as replica and passes as primary, automatically rerouting. (3) The application writes to port 5432 (primary), reads from port 5433 (replicas, load-balanced). (4) Add `maxconn` per server to prevent connection pool exhaustion. (5) Use `option pgsql-check` (HAProxy has a built-in PostgreSQL check since 1.5) if you don't want a custom tcp-check. PgBouncer is often used in front of HAProxy to pool connections — HAProxy load-balances between PgBouncer instances, which pool to PostgreSQL.
**Visual:**
```
app writes -> HAProxy:5432 -> pg_primary (pg1, checked via transaction_read_only=off)
app reads  -> HAProxy:5433 -> pg_replicas (pg2, pg3, pg4, RR, checked via =on)

if pg1 fails:
  - promote pg2 to primary (e.g., via Patroni)
  - HAProxy's tcp-check on pg2: "r/w" -> matches primary
  - HAProxy routes writes to pg2 automatically
  - (need to remove pg2 from replicas pool, or run-time API)
```

### Q5. HAProxy is restarting unexpectedly under high load. How do you diagnose?
**Answer:** HAProxy restarts (crashes) are rare — its bug rate is famously low — so when it happens, suspect environmental issues first. (1) **OOM kill** — check `dmesg | grep -i oom` and `journalctl -u haproxy`; if HAProxy's `maxconn` is set very high (e.g., 1M) and connections are accumulating, the per-connection memory can exhaust RAM, triggering the OOM killer. Reduce `maxconn` to a realistic value, increase RAM, or scale out. (2) **File descriptor exhaustion** — `ulimit -n` and `fs.file-max` must be high enough; with 100K connections, HAProxy needs 200K+ FDs (client + backend). Check `cat /proc/<haproxy_pid>/limits`. (3) **CPU starvation** — if HAProxy is single-threaded (default) and a CPU core is saturated by another process, HAProxy can't process connections fast enough and may time out; check `top -H`. Use `nbthread N` to use multiple cores. (4) **Bug in HAProxy itself** — check the HAProxy version against known CVEs and bug fixes; upgrade to the latest stable. (5) **Segfault from a misbehaving backend** — rare, but a backend sending malformed responses (e.g., huge headers exceeding `tune.bufsize`) can trigger edge cases. (6) **Kernel-level issues** — `conntrack` table full, `nf_conntrack` dropping packets; check `dmesg`. (7) **Config reload race** — if you're reloading frequently, the old and new processes can briefly conflict; check for reload storms. The standard debugging flow: `journalctl -u haproxy`, `dmesg`, `cat /proc/<pid>/limits`, `top -H -p <pid>`, then HAProxy's own logs.
**Visual:**
```
journalctl -u haproxy:
  haproxy[1234]: exited with status 137   <- OOM kill (137 = 128 + 9 SIGKILL)

dmesg:
  Out of memory: Killed process 1234 (haproxy) total-vm:8GB

fix: reduce maxconn (1M -> 100K), increase RAM, or scale out (more HAProxy)
     check ulimit -n (should be > 2x maxconn)
     nbthread N (use multiple CPU cores)
```

### Q6. You want to use HAProxy as an API gateway with path-based routing, JWT validation, and rate limiting. How would you architect this?
**Answer:** HAProxy can be a capable API gateway with the right configuration, though for heavy logic you may want to add Lua. Architecture: (1) **Frontend** with `bind *:443 ssl crt ...` for SSL termination, then ACL-based routing: `acl is_users path_beg /api/users`, `acl is_orders path_beg /api/orders`, `use_backend users_svc if is_users`, etc. (2) **JWT validation** — HAProxy 2.1+ has built-in JWT support via `http-request set-var(txn.valid_jwt) jwt_header_verify(...)`; for older versions, use Lua (`lua-load /etc/haproxy/jwt.lua`) or external auth via `http-request lua.auth` or `http-request set-header X-Auth-Result %[lua.jwt_check()]`. Reject with `http-request deny if !{ var(txn.valid_jwt) -m bool }`. (3) **Rate limiting** — use stick-tables: `stick-table type ip size 100k expire 30s store http_req_rate(10s)` per-frontend, then `http-request deny if { src_http_req_rate gt 100 }` to limit per-IP. For per-user rate limits, key on a header (e.g., `Authorization` or `X-User-ID`) instead of `src`. (4) **Stats and observability** — `stats enable`, plus `log` to syslog for access logs, and Prometheus exporter (`haproxy_exporter`) for metrics. (5) **Hot reload + runtime API** for adding new routes/services without downtime. Trade-off: HAProxy as API gateway is fast and lightweight but lacks the rich plugin ecosystem of Kong or Apigee; for complex transformations (XML-to-JSON, response rewriting), use Lua or pair HAProxy with a sidecar like Envoy. Many teams use HAProxy for L4/L7 routing + rate limiting + JWT, and a separate service (the app itself or a sidecar) for richer transformations.
**Visual:**
```
frontend api_gateway
  bind *:443 ssl crt /certs/api.pem
  acl is_users  path_beg /api/users
  acl is_orders path_beg /api/orders
  http-request lua.jwt_check      # set txn.valid_jwt
  http-request deny if !{ var(txn.valid_jwt) -m bool }
  stick-table type ip size 100k expire 30s store http_req_rate(10s)
  http-request deny if { src_http_req_rate gt 100 }
  use_backend users_svc if is_users
  use_backend orders_svc if is_orders

stats: /haproxy?stats        runtime: /run/haproxy/admin.sock
Prometheus: haproxy_exporter -> Grafana
```

### Q7. You're migrating from F5 hardware load balancers to HAProxy. What differences and gotchas should you expect?
**Answer:** Several. (1) **Performance model** — F5 hardware has dedicated ASICs for SSL/TLS and connection handling, so even a small F5 can sustain 10s of Gbps of TLS traffic; HAProxy is software running on general-purpose CPUs, so equivalent throughput requires a beefy server (multi-core, AES-NI, fast NICs) or scaling out (multiple HAProxy instances). Plan capacity carefully. (2) **iRules vs Lua** — F5's iRules (Tcl-based) for custom logic translate to HAProxy's Lua scripting or simpler `http-request` rules; complex iRules need rewrites. (3) **Configuration model** — F5 has a web UI and a rich REST API (iControl); HAProxy is text-config (`haproxy.cfg`) plus the runtime socket API. The shift from GUI-driven config to text-driven config is a cultural change but is generally welcome (version-controlled, code-reviewed). (4) **SSL cert management** — F5 has a cert management UI; HAProxy uses files in a directory (`/etc/haproxy/certs/`) with the `crt` directive listing them. Automate via cert-manager + a small script that combines key+cert into the PEM format HAProxy expects. (5) **Health checks** — F5 has sophisticated monitors (HTTP, HTTPS, TCP, EAV, external scripts); HAProxy's `option httpchk`, `tcp-check`, and `agent-check` cover most cases but external-script monitors need a small agent running on the backend. (6) **Persistence** — F5 has many persistence types (cookie, source-IP, SSL session ID, universal); HAProxy has `stick-table` (cookie, source-IP, header, SSL session ID) covering the common cases. (7) **Failover / HA** — F5 has built-in active-standby pairs via config-sync; HAProxy uses Keepalived (VRRP) or PaceMaker for active-standby, or you run active-active with DNS/anycast. Plan the HA topology carefully — it's the biggest operational change. (8) **Support** — F5 has vendor support and SLAs; HAProxy has community + HAProxy Enterprise (commercial) support. The migration is mechanical but requires careful testing, especially for iRules and HA topology.
**Visual:**
```
F5 hardware                    HAProxy software
  iRules (Tcl)          ->     Lua or http-request rules
  Web UI / REST         ->     text config + runtime socket
  Built-in HA pairs     ->     Keepalived (VRRP) or DNS
  Cert UI               ->     /etc/haproxy/certs/ + automation
  Vendor support        ->     community + HAProxy Enterprise

capacity planning: F5 ASIC -> multi-core CPU + AES-NI + scale-out
HA:              F5 active-standby -> Keepalived or active-active
```

quiz.explanation: Both HAProxy and NGINX do zero-downtime reloads, but HAProxy's mechanism is more transparent. systemctl reload haproxy causes the master process to re-exec with the new config. The new process inherits the listening sockets from the old process (via SO_REUSEPORT or the fd@ inherit-fd mechanism), so the new process is immediately ready to accept connections on the same port.
